newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines sees deliberate attacks on peso.
newsitem.headline: Philippines sees deliberate attacks on peso.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos on Wednesday attacked what he said was a foreign campaign to undermine the peso after reports of a possible devaluation battered the country's financial markets.
The stock market took its steepest fall in three months and the Central Bank dumped an estimated $300 million to fend off a fresh attack on the peso.

"The unusual behaviour of the exchange rate as well as the obvious attacks on the peso...indicate that there could be a deliberate effort to undermine the peso from outside sources," Ramos told his weekly news conference.
The latest effort to unseat the peso follows a Singapore Straits Times report quoting a Philippine minister -- who denied any such comment -- saying the government might devalue.

Earlier this week, a report in the same newspaper, quoting a different minister also talking about a possible devaluation, forced the central bank to sell dollars and boost interest rates to a 2-1/2 year high. The minister also denied the report.
"We are also seeing a media disinformation campaign of some kind," Ramos said.

The Philippines insists its economy, which it hopes will soon be the next Asian tiger, has the underlying strength to win any battles with speculators and not take the same path as Thailand, which was forced into a de facto devaluation last week.
For nearly two years the government has maintained what it calls a market-oriented peso policy. Traders call it a heavily managed flotation.
Whatever the terminology, it is a central plank of the government policy of keeping inflation low, and the peso has barely changed in value against the dollar since late-1995.
The policy-making Monetary Board said it had no intention of changing tack, and warned it would punish speculators.
"The (Central Bank) will intervene strongly using all its available policy weapons to maintain an orderly foreign exchange market and to penalise speculators," a Board statement said.
It noted that first quarter gross national product was up a strong 6.1 percent, while inflation fell to 4.6 percent in the first half of the year.
Despite government denials, investors remain worried that the Philippines has been tainted by Thailand's financial crisis.

"The market is very jittery. It believes there may be some truth in these peso devaluation rumours. Overseas investors, who took positions in the peso believing it would be strong, are panicking," the treasurer at one leading foreign bank said.

"All these comparisons between the Philippines if looked at closely show the resemblance is not so close, but since we are in the same region and an emerging market we are caught in all these uncertainties," he said.
Share prices closed just over four percent lower in their sharpest drop since April when the market was also battered by fears of a spillover from the financial problems in Thailand.
The peso also came under renewed pressure from speculators, forcing the Central Bank to dump at least $300 million.
Analysts warn that the peso defensive measures are beginning to take their toll and that high interest rates, if they go on too long, will start to hurt industry in the Philippines.

"Businesses are legitimately screaming bloody murder now. The Central bank has certainly shown a willingness to ignore the domestic economy in defence of the peso," Scott Wilson, economist with Chase Manhattan Bank in Hong Kong, said.
Bankers said that so far the peso is probably safe but there is a danger if major companies start to lose their nerve.
One sign would be if they switched their loans from dollars to pesos. If there are prospects of a devaluation it would make more sense to do loans in pesos.
"So far, I haven't seen that. There hasn't been any wave of alarm from local conglomerates," Bank of America global capital markets managing director in Manila, Jaime Panganiban said.
